subject: Science
source: National Curriculum KS2 Science (Plants; Animals including humans); Drive Science folder 'Science lower school' (3.8 organisms) | Spring 1 2027 (lessons 9 to 18): Tarbiyyah Primary Year 3 curriculum map and Science Long Term Plan 2023-24 (Cornerstones Mighty Metals and Why Do Cat's Eyes Glow at Night?), home practicals with household items

lessons.title: Parts of a flowering plant and their jobs
objectives: Name the main parts of a flowering plant
Describe the function of roots, stem, leaves and flower
Label a diagram accurately

keywords.def: anchors the plant and takes in water and minerals from the soil
supports the plant and carries water and nutrients
uses sunlight to make food for the plant
the part of the plant that makes seeds

starter: Bismillah. Name two parts of a plant you learned in Year 2 or Year 1.
What is the difference between a deciduous and an evergreen tree?
What do all living things need to survive?

teach.heading: Roots
bullets: Roots hold the plant in the soil
teach.note: Show a clear photo of a plant with roots visible. Ask 'What would happen in a strong wind if a tree had no roots?' Roots anchor the plant.

teach.heading: Stem
bullets: The stem holds up leaves and flowers
It carries food around the plant
teach.note: Compare the stem to a straw carrying a drink. Some stems are woody (trees), some soft (daisies).

teach.heading: Leaves
bullets: They make food for the plant
teach.note: Introduce the word photosynthesis only; detail comes in Year 5/6. Misconception: plants take food from soil. They make their own food in leaves.

teach.heading: Flower
teach.note: Show a labelled flower photo. Link to Qur'an 6:99: Allah sends down rain and brings forth plants. Keep it as a reflection, not as science content.

teach.heading: Labelling practice
teach.note: Model one label and function on the board. Safe demo: use a pot plant or herb (mint, basil) at home. Look, do not eat.

practice: Which part of the plant takes in water: root or flower?
A sunflower has fallen over. Which part has failed to hold it up, the root or the stem? Explain.
Match each part to its job: root, stem, leaf, flower.
independent: Draw and label a flowering plant with root, stem, leaf and flower. Write the function of each next to the label.
Explain in two sentences why leaves are important to the plant.
Compare a tree and a daisy: write two things that are the same and two that are different.
exit: What is the job of the stem?
lessons.homework: Look at a plant at home. Draw it and label its roots (if you can see them), stem, leaves and any flower.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a labelled diagram and a word bank with pictures. Stretch: explain why a cactus has thick stems and few leaves.

lessons.title: What plants need to grow
objectives: State what plants need to grow healthily: light, water, air, suitable temperature and space
Plan a fair test about plant growth
Predict and explain what will happen if one need is removed

keywords.def: substances in soil that plants need to stay healthy
an investigation where only one thing is changed
something that can be changed or measured
when a seed starts to grow

starter: Bismillah. Name the four main parts of a flowering plant.
What does a leaf do?
What do you need to grow healthily?

teach.heading: Needs of a plant
teach.note: Ask children to predict what happens if each is missing. Link to Qur'an 21:30 (Allah made every living thing from water): water is essential for life.

teach.heading: Testing one thing at a time
teach.note: Explain fair testing with a simple question: does light help cress grow? Change = light. Keep same = water, soil, seeds, temperature.

teach.heading: Setting up the investigation
bullets: Pot B: no light, same water
teach.note: Safe practical at home: grow cress or beans on damp kitchen paper; one in a cupboard, one on a windowsill. No chemicals. Watch the results over the next lessons and compare by video call.

teach.heading: Predicting
teach.note: Teach 'I predict ... because ...'. Plants kept in the dark grow tall and pale as they search for light. Avoid claiming they grow 'fast'; they are weak.

practice: Name the variable we change in the cress investigation.
Name two variables we must keep the same.
Predict what will happen to the plant in the cupboard. Use 'because'.
independent: Write a plan for an investigation: Does water affect how a bean plant grows? Include what you change, what you measure and two things you keep the same.
Draw a results table with columns: day, plant A height (cm), plant B height (cm).
Explain why a fair test is important.
exit: Name three things plants need to grow.
In a fair test, how many things do we change?
lessons.homework: Set up your cress investigation at home with a grown-up and measure its height each day for a week.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a planning frame with sentence starters. Stretch: suggest how to measure the plants more accurately.

lessons.title: How water moves through a plant
objectives: Describe how water travels from roots to leaves
Observe an investigation showing water moving up a stem
Record observations and explain them

keywords.def: to move something from one place to another
to take in
to change from a liquid to a gas
narrow channels inside a stem that carry water

starter: Bismillah. Name three things plants need to grow.
Which part of the plant takes in water?
What does the stem do?

teach.heading: Water journey
teach.note: Draw the journey as an arrow from root to stem to leaf. Ask 'How does water get to the top of a tall tree?' Tiny tubes in the stem.

teach.heading: Tubes in the stem
teach.note: Water evaporates from leaves and pulls more water up, like sucking a drink through a straw. Keep it simple at this level.

teach.heading: Coloured water investigation
bullets: Look for colour in the leaves
teach.note: Safe at-home demo using food colouring in a glass of water and a celery stick or white carnation; a grown-up helps. Do not drink the water. If no celery at home, show a time-lapse video.

teach.heading: Observing and explaining
teach.note: A grown-up cuts across the celery (or show a photo). The coloured dots show where the water has travelled. Ask 'What do the dots tell us?'

practice: Put these in order: leaf, root, stem. Show the journey of water.
Why did the celery leaves change colour?
What would happen if we cut the stem off the plant?
independent: Draw a labelled diagram showing the path of water through a plant from soil to leaf.
Write a paragraph beginning: 'The coloured water moved up the celery because ...'
Predict what would happen with a different food colouring and explain.
exit: Which part of the plant takes in water?
How does water reach the leaves?
lessons.homework: Record what happened in your celery or flower experiment. Draw before and after pictures.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a pre-drawn plant to label and arrows to follow. Stretch: explain why a wilting plant recovers when watered.

lessons.title: Pollination, seeds and the life cycle of a flowering plant
objectives: Describe pollination and seed dispersal
Order the stages in the life cycle of a flowering plant
Name ways seeds are spread

keywords.def: tiny grains from a flower that help make seeds
when pollen is moved to another flower
spreading seeds away from the parent plant
the stages a living thing goes through from birth to making young

starter: Bismillah. How does water move up a stem?
Which part of a plant makes seeds?
What happens to a seed when it gets water and warmth?

teach.heading: Pollination
bullets: Insects carry pollen to another flower
teach.note: Show a bee on a flower photo. Colourful petals and nectar attract insects. Some flowers use wind. Ask 'Why are petals bright?'

teach.heading: Seeds and fruit
bullets: The flower can become a fruit
teach.note: Safe demo: cut an apple or pepper with an adult and find the seeds. Ask what the seeds can become.

teach.heading: Seed dispersal
teach.note: Show photos or videos. Why disperse? To avoid crowding and find new places to grow.

teach.heading: Life cycle
teach.note: Draw it as a circle. Seeds need water and warmth to germinate; light is needed later for growth. Common misconception: seeds need light to germinate (most do not).

practice: Put these in order: flower, seed, germination, new seeds.
How might a dandelion seed be dispersed?
Why are some flowers brightly coloured?
independent: Draw the life cycle of a flowering plant as a circle with labels.
Match each seed to how it is dispersed: sycamore, burdock, coconut, dandelion.
Explain why seeds are spread away from the parent plant.
exit: Name one way seeds are dispersed.
lessons.homework: Draw and label the life cycle of a bean or sunflower plant from seed to seed.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide sequencing cards with pictures. Stretch: explain what could go wrong if there were no pollinators.

lessons.title: Nutrition and food groups
objectives: Explain why animals including humans need nutrition
Name the main food groups and give examples
Explain that animals cannot make their own food

keywords.def: the food and nutrients animals need to live and grow
foods that give energy, such as bread and rice
food for growth and repair, such as fish and beans
foods that store energy and keep us warm, like oil

starter: Bismillah. Say the stages in a plant's life cycle.
Why can't animals make their own food like plants do?
What did you have for breakfast?

teach.heading: Why we need food
teach.note: Ask 'What happens if a car has no fuel?' compare to a body with no food. Animals cannot make their own food, so they eat plants or other animals.

teach.heading: Food groups
teach.note: Show photos. Link to Qur'an 7:31 (eat and drink, but do not be wasteful). Keep ethos light: we thank Allah for food by saying Bismillah before eating and Alhamdulillah after.

teach.heading: Vitamins, minerals, fibre and water
bullets: Vitamins and minerals keep us healthy
teach.note: Fruit and vegetables give vitamins; milk gives calcium for bones. Misconception: fat is always bad; we need some fat.

teach.heading: Sorting foods
bullets: Some foods fit more than one group
teach.note: Safe task: children look through the kitchen cupboards (with a grown-up) and read labels, or use pictures. Do not taste unknown items. Check allergies.

practice: Which food group does rice belong to?
Name a food that gives us protein.
Why do we need water every day?
independent: Sort 12 foods (such as bread, egg, apple, olive oil, lentils, fish, rice, yoghurt, nuts, carrot, pasta, beans) into food groups.
Write two sentences: why do animals need food?
Design a healthy lunch for a child and label the food groups in it.
exit: Name the food group that gives energy.
Why can't animals make their own food?
lessons.homework: Record everything you eat at lunch and dinner and sort it into food groups.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use picture sorting cards with key words. Stretch: explain why athletes may need more carbohydrates.

lessons.title: A balanced diet
objectives: Explain what a balanced diet is
Use a plate model to plan a balanced meal
Explain how too much or too little of a food group affects health

keywords.def: eating the right amounts of different types of food
the amount of a food you eat in one meal
being well and strong in your body and mind
eating or doing something without going to extremes

starter: Bismillah. Name three food groups.
Which food group gives most energy?
What do vitamins do?

teach.heading: What is a balanced diet?
bullets: A mix of all food groups
teach.note: No single food gives everything. Use the Eatwell plate idea in simple form: about a third fruit and veg, a third starchy foods, protein, some dairy, a little fat and sugar.

teach.heading: Eating in moderation
teach.note: The Prophet (peace be upon him) taught moderation in eating: a third for food, a third for drink and a third for air (recorded by Tirmidhi). Also cite Qur'an 7:31 on not being wasteful.

teach.heading: Too much or too little
bullets: Too little food: tired and weak
Too much sugar: bad for teeth
teach.note: Handle sensitively; avoid body-shaming. Focus on energy, teeth and growing strong. Link to being thankful for food and sharing with those in need.

teach.heading: Plan a meal
teach.note: Model a meal: rice, chicken or lentils, salad, and fruit. Check dietary rules in line with halal. Ask children to explain why the plate is balanced.

practice: Is a plate of only chips a balanced meal? Explain.
Add one food to this meal to make it more balanced: rice and chicken.
Why should we drink water instead of sugary drinks most days?
independent: Draw a plate divided into sections and plan a balanced dinner. Label each food group.
Write a short explanation of why a balanced diet is important.
Make a poster with three tips for eating well.
exit: Name one food that helps our bones and one that gives energy.
lessons.homework: Plan a balanced family dinner and explain why it is balanced.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a plate template and food pictures. Stretch: compare two children's meals and suggest improvements.

lessons.title: Skeletons and bones
objectives: Describe three functions of a skeleton: support, protection and movement
Name main bones such as skull, ribs, spine and femur
Compare human skeletons with animal skeletons

keywords.def: the bones inside the body that support and protect it
the bones of the head that protect the brain
curved bones that protect the heart and lungs
small bones that make up the backbone

starter: Bismillah. What is a balanced diet?
Which food helps keep our bones strong?
Can you feel any bones in your body? Where?

teach.heading: Three jobs of a skeleton
teach.note: Ask 'What would you look like with no skeleton?' (floppy like a jellyfish). Show a skeleton picture.

teach.heading: Main bones
teach.note: Children feel their own ribs and spine safely. A baby has about 300 bones; adults have 206 as some join together. Use only if confident; both facts are accurate.

teach.heading: Animal skeletons
teach.note: Compare a fish, a bird, a snail and a beetle. Beetles have an exoskeleton on the outside; snails have shells. Do not overload.

teach.heading: Investigating bones
teach.note: Safe activity: children measure arm and leg lengths with a ruler or string. Record in a table; discuss who has the longest femur (thigh bone) relative to their body.

practice: Which bones protect the heart and lungs?
Name the three jobs of the skeleton.
Is a snail a vertebrate or an invertebrate? Explain.
independent: Draw and label a human skeleton with skull, ribs, spine, arm and leg bones.
Write a sentence for each job of the skeleton.
Sort these animals into vertebrates and invertebrates: dog, worm, fish, spider, bird.
exit: Name one job of the skeleton.
lessons.homework: Find out the name of one more bone in the body and what it does.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a skeleton picture with a word bank. Stretch: explain why a snail needs a shell but a human does not.

lessons.title: Muscles, joints and movement
objectives: Explain that muscles pull on bones to move the body
Identify joints such as the elbow and knee
Describe how pairs of muscles work together

keywords.def: body tissue that pulls to make parts of the body move
a place where two bones meet
to get shorter and tighter
to become loose and longer again

starter: Bismillah. Name three jobs of the skeleton.
Which bones protect the lungs?
How do we bend our arm?

teach.heading: Muscles move bones
teach.note: Misconception: muscles push bones. They only pull by contracting. Use a model with elastic bands if available, or a video.

teach.heading: Pairs of muscles
bullets: When one contracts the other relaxes
teach.note: Children feel the biceps at the front of the upper arm as they bend the elbow. Demonstrate the pair working together.

teach.heading: Joints
teach.note: Children move elbow and shoulder to feel the difference. Hinge moves one way like a door; ball and socket moves in many directions.

teach.heading: Keeping muscles and bones strong
teach.note: Link to healthy habits and prayer movements as gentle exercise if appropriate. Safe movement activity: warm-up shown on screen, children move only within a safe space.

practice: Which muscle contracts when you bend your arm?
Is the knee a hinge joint or a ball and socket joint?
What happens to the triceps when the biceps contracts?
independent: Draw the arm bending and straightening, labelling biceps, triceps and bones.
Make a table of joints you can find in your body and the type of movement each allows.
Write two sentences explaining how muscles and bones work together.
lessons.homework: Find three joints in your body and describe how each one moves.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use a model arm and an annotated picture. Stretch: explain why we need pairs of muscles.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Forces, magnets and light (Mighty Metals and Why Do Cat's Eyes Glow at Night?)
lessons.title: Friction: why do things slow down?
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a toy car stop on a carpet but roll far on a smooth floor?
objectives: To understand that friction is a force that slows moving things down
successCriteria: All: say that friction is a force between two surfaces
Most: predict which surface gives more friction
Some: explain why rough surfaces slow things more than smooth ones
lessons.smsc: Social: taking turns and sharing equipment safely at home

keywords.def: a push or a pull
a force that slows things when two surfaces rub
the top or outside layer of something
bumpy, not smooth
flat and even, with no bumps

hook.text: Why is it easy to slide in socks on a shiny floor but hard on a carpet?
hook.a: The carpet is rough, so there is more friction. The shiny floor is smooth, so there is less.

islamicLink.text: Allah made the earth firm under our feet so we can walk on it. Allah says He made the earth a resting place for us (al-Baqarah 2:22). Friction is part of this mercy: without it we could not walk, hold a cup or stop a bike.

starter.q: Is a kick a push or a pull?
Name one force that pulls things down to the ground.
Opening a drawer: push or pull?

teach.heading: What is friction?
bullets: It happens when two surfaces rub
teach.note: Rub your hands together fast. Ask: what do you feel? Warmth and a grip. That grip is friction.

teach.heading: Rough and smooth
bullets: More friction means a shorter journey
teach.note: Show a towel and a tray on camera. Ask pupils to touch two surfaces at home and say which is rougher.

teach.heading: Friction helps us
teach.note: Ask: where is friction useful in your home? Where is it a nuisance, like a sticking door?

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Give 30 seconds, then share results.

check.q: A toy car rolls on four surfaces. Where will it go furthest?
check.why: The smooth floor has the least friction, so the car travels furthest.

practice.q: A ball rolls on grass and on a smooth path. Where does it stop sooner?
practice.a: On the grass: it is rougher, so there is more friction.
practice.model: Think: which surface is rougher? Grass is rougher. Rough means more friction. More friction slows the ball sooner. So it stops sooner on the grass.

practice.q: Is friction a push or a pull, or something else?
practice.a: It is a force that works against movement (it pushes back against the way something moves).

practice.q: Name one place where friction is useful.
practice.a: For example: shoe soles, bike brakes, tyres, holding a pencil.

independent.q: Core: Push a toy car or a small box across three surfaces at home (a towel, the floor, a tray). Write them in order, most friction first.
independent.a: For example: towel, floor, tray (rough to smooth).
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: same toy, same gentle push, three surfaces. Most friction is where it stops soonest.

independent.q: Extend: Why did the toy stop soonest on the roughest surface?
independent.a: Rough surfaces rub more, so there is more friction slowing it.

independent.q: Stretch: Why do people put salt or grit on icy paths?
independent.a: To make the path rougher, so shoes get more friction and people do not slip.

exit.q: Which gives more friction? A) a towel B) a tray
exit.a: A) a towel

exit.q: Big question: why does a toy car stop on a carpet but roll far on a smooth floor?
exit.a: The carpet is rough, so there is more friction slowing the car.

lessons.homework: Find three things at home that use friction to help us (for example shoe soles) and draw or write them in your book.
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards of surfaces to sort into rough and smooth. EAL: rough, smooth, slow with pictures. Stretch: think of a place where we want less friction and how we make it smoother.

lessons.title: Friction fair test: the ramp investigation
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we make our friction test fair?
objectives: To understand how to run a fair test to compare friction on different surfaces
successCriteria: All: measure how far a toy rolls off a ramp
Most: keep the ramp, toy and push the same each time
Some: use the results table to write a conclusion
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: measuring in centimetres and reading a table
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty: recording what really happened, not what we hoped

keywords.def: a test where we change only one thing
find out how big or long something is
a slope for things to roll down
what we found out
a force that slows things when surfaces rub

hook.text: If you rolled a toy car down a ramp onto a towel and pushed it harder than on the floor, would it be a fair race?
hook.a: No. Only one thing should change: the surface. The push must stay the same.

starter.q: What is friction?
starter.a: A force that slows things when two surfaces rub.

starter.q: Which has more friction? A) ice B) carpet
Write 1 m in centimetres.

teach.heading: Our question
bullets: Which surface lets the car roll furthest?
teach.note: Build the ramp live: a tray resting on two books. Point out what we will keep the same.

teach.heading: Keep it fair
teach.note: Ask: what would happen if we pushed the car on one surface? It would not be fair.

teach.heading: Safety first
bullets: Ask an adult before moving books
Keep the toy away from stairs
teach.note: Read the safety card together. Tidy away when finished.

teach.heading: Record in a table
teach.note: Model the table on screen.

practice.q: From the table, which surface let the car roll furthest?
practice.a: The floor (120 cm and 116 cm).
practice.model: Look down the columns for the biggest numbers. Floor: 120 and 116. These are the biggest, so the car went furthest on the floor.

practice.q: Which surface had the most friction?
practice.a: The towel: the car only rolled about 30 cm.

practice.q: Name one thing we kept the same.
practice.a: For example: the same car, the same ramp height, letting go without pushing.

independent.q: Core: Do the ramp test at home on 3 surfaces (floor, paper, a towel or cardboard). Record two goes each in your table.
independent.a: Pupils' own results; the towel usually gives the shortest distance.
independent.model: Teacher shows one go on camera: put the car at the top line, let go, measure from the ramp end to the front of the car with a ruler or tape, write it down.

independent.q: Extend: Write a conclusion: 'The car rolled furthest on ... because ...'
independent.a: For example: The car rolled furthest on the floor because it is smooth and has the least friction.

independent.q: Stretch: Why did we do each surface twice?
independent.a: To check our results; if the two goes are close, we can trust them more.

exit.q: In a fair test, how many things do we change? A) one B) two C) all of them
exit.a: A) one

exit.q: Big question: how can we make our friction test fair?
exit.a: Change only the surface; keep the car, ramp height and release the same.

lessons.homework: Finish your ramp table and write one sentence about which surface had the most friction.
lessons.send: SEND: a ready-made table and a partner adult to measure. EAL: same, change, measure with gestures. Stretch: predict what happens if the ramp is made higher, and why.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Forces, magnets and light (Mighty Metals and Why Do Cat's Eyes Glow at Night?)
lessons.title: Magnetic and non-magnetic materials
lessons.bigQuestion: What makes something stick to a magnet?
objectives: To understand that only some materials are magnetic
successCriteria: All: sort objects into magnetic and non-magnetic
Most: say that magnetic objects contain iron or steel
Some: explain why not all metals are magnetic
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and technology: magnetic catches on doors and lunch boxes
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the hidden forces Allah placed in creation

keywords.def: an object that pulls iron and steel towards it
pulled by a magnet
not pulled by a magnet
what something is made of
a hard, shiny material such as iron or copper

hook.text: Is every metal pulled by a magnet? How could you find out at home?
hook.a: No. Test spoons, foil, coins and cans with a fridge magnet and see.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'And We sent down iron, in which is great strength and benefits for people' (al-Hadid 57:25). Iron is the main metal that magnets pull, and we use it in tools, buildings and magnets.

starter.q: What does friction do to a moving toy?
In a fair test, how many things do we change?
Name a metal.
starter.a: For example: iron, steel, copper, aluminium, gold.

teach.heading: What do magnets do?
teach.note: Hold a fridge magnet to a paper clip on camera. Then to a pencil. Ask what is different.

teach.heading: Make a prediction
teach.note: Show a spoon, a coin, foil, a key. Pupils predict before you test.

teach.heading: Sort the objects
teach.note: Read each card. Pupils show 1 or 2 on fingers.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Give 30 seconds, then share results.

check.why: Steel contains iron, so the paper clip is pulled by the magnet.

practice.q: Is a wooden spoon magnetic?
practice.a: No, wood is non-magnetic.
practice.model: Ask: is it made of iron or steel? Wood is not. So the magnet will not pull it. It is non-magnetic.

practice.q: Is a steel spoon magnetic?
practice.a: Yes, most steel is magnetic because it contains iron.

practice.q: Finish: 'Magnetic objects are usually made of ...'
practice.a: iron or steel

independent.q: Core: Test 8 objects at home with a fridge magnet. Sort them in a two-column table: magnetic and non-magnetic.
independent.a: Pupils' own; steel and iron objects are magnetic, plastic, wood, glass and fabric are not.
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: hold the magnet close to a key, a sock and a tin. Write each in the right column.

independent.q: Extend: Did any results surprise you? Write one.
independent.a: For example: foil is a metal but was not magnetic.

independent.q: Stretch: Write a rule that fits all your results.
independent.a: For example: things made of iron or steel are magnetic; other materials are not.

exit.q: Are all metals magnetic? A) yes B) no
exit.a: B) no

exit.q: Big question: what makes something stick to a magnet?
exit.a: It is made of a magnetic material such as iron or steel.

lessons.homework: Find five magnetic things on your fridge or around your kitchen (with an adult) and list them.
lessons.send: SEND: real objects and a two-hoop sort. EAL: magnet, magnetic, non-magnetic with pictures. Stretch: test a coin and say what it might be made of.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Forces, magnets and light (Mighty Metals and Why Do Cat's Eyes Glow at Night?)
lessons.title: Which metals are magnetic? The kitchen sort
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a magnet pick up a steel spoon but not an aluminium can?
objectives: To understand that iron and steel are magnetic but metals such as aluminium and copper are not
successCriteria: All: name iron and steel as magnetic metals
Most: sort kitchen metals into magnetic and non-magnetic
Some: use a magnet to sort cans for recycling and explain how it works
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: how recycling centres sort metals
lessons.smsc: Moral: looking after Allah's earth by recycling and not wasting

keywords.def: a strong metal that magnets pull
a metal made mostly from iron
a light metal that magnets do not pull
an orange-brown metal that magnets do not pull
use materials again to make new things

hook.text: A recycling centre has a huge pile of mixed cans. How could a magnet help to sort them?
hook.a: Steel cans stick to a big magnet; aluminium cans do not, so they can be separated.

islamicLink.text: Allah taught the Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) to work with iron and make coats of armour (Saba 34:10-11). Learning which metals are strong and magnetic helps us use Allah's gifts wisely.

starter.q: Is plastic magnetic?
Name a magnetic metal.
What is the opposite of magnetic?

teach.heading: Not all metals
teach.note: Show a foil sheet: shiny metal, but the magnet does not pull it.

teach.heading: Kitchen metals
teach.note: Ask pupils which they might find in their own kitchen.

teach.heading: Sorting cans
teach.note: Explain recycling centres use giant magnets on conveyor belts.
cycle: A big magnet lifts steel cans
Aluminium cans stay on the belt
Each metal is melted and reused

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds, then share results.

check.q: Which can will a magnet pick up?
check.why: Steel contains iron, so it is magnetic. Aluminium and copper are metals but not magnetic.

practice.q: Is aluminium foil magnetic?
practice.a: No. Aluminium is a metal but it is not magnetic.
practice.model: Step 1: what metal is it? Aluminium. Step 2: is aluminium magnetic? No. So foil is not pulled by a magnet.

practice.q: Is a steel food tin magnetic?
practice.a: Yes, steel contains iron.

practice.q: True or false: all shiny metals are magnetic.
practice.a: False: aluminium and copper are shiny but not magnetic.

independent.q: Core: With an adult, test 6 metal things in the kitchen (tin, foil, spoon, pan, key, coin). Record magnetic or not.
independent.a: Pupils' own; steel tins and most steel spoons are magnetic, foil is not.
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: test a tin (sticks: steel) and foil (does not stick: aluminium). Write both in the table.

independent.q: Extend: Explain how a magnet could sort steel and aluminium cans.
independent.a: The magnet pulls the steel cans out; the aluminium cans are left behind.

independent.q: Stretch: A pan is not pulled by the magnet. What metal might it be? Why?
independent.a: Aluminium or copper, because those metals are not magnetic.

exit.q: Which metal is NOT magnetic? A) iron B) steel C) aluminium
exit.a: C) aluminium

exit.q: Big question: why does a magnet pick up a steel spoon but not an aluminium can?
exit.a: Steel contains iron, which is magnetic; aluminium is not.

lessons.send: SEND: real cans and foil to test, with picture labels. EAL: iron, steel, aluminium, copper on a word mat. Stretch: find out why steel tins are used for food.

lessons.title: Magnets attract and repel: poles
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a magnet push something without touching it?
objectives: To understand that magnets have two poles and can attract or repel without touching
successCriteria: All: name the north and south poles of a magnet
Most: say that like poles repel and unlike poles attract
Some: show that magnetic forces act at a distance and through paper
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: the north and south of a compass
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at an invisible force we cannot see but can feel

keywords.def: the end of a magnet where the force is strongest
pull towards
push away
one end of a magnet, often marked N
the other end of a magnet, often marked S

hook.text: You can feel two magnets push apart, but there is nothing between them. What is pushing?
hook.a: The magnetic force acts at a distance. It does not need touching.

starter.q: Is a steel paper clip magnetic?
Name a metal that is not magnetic.
What is a force?

teach.heading: Two poles
bullets: Every magnet has a north and a south pole
The force is strongest at the poles
teach.note: Show a bar magnet with N and S. Paper clips cling most at the ends.

teach.heading: Attract or repel?
bullets: Like poles repel: N and N, S and S
Unlike poles attract: N and S
teach.note: If pupils have two fridge magnets, try them back to back.

teach.heading: Force at a distance
bullets: Magnets do not need to touch
teach.note: Hold a paper clip under paper, move a magnet above it. The clip moves. Contact forces, like friction, need touching.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds, then share results.

check.q: Two north poles are brought together. What happens?

practice.q: N and S are put together. Attract or repel?
practice.a: Attract (unlike poles).
practice.model: Are the poles the same or different? N and S are different. Different poles attract. So they pull together.

practice.q: S and S are put together. Attract or repel?
practice.a: Repel (like poles).

practice.q: Does a magnet need to touch a paper clip to move it?
practice.a: No: magnetic force acts at a distance.

independent.q: Core: Put a paper clip on paper. Move a magnet underneath without touching the clip. Write what happens.
independent.a: The paper clip moves with the magnet: the force works through the paper.
independent.model: Teacher shows it first on camera, then pupils try it.

independent.q: Extend: Try through 1, 2, then 5 sheets of paper. Does it still work?
independent.a: It works through a few sheets but gets weaker as the gap grows.

independent.q: Stretch: Why might a magnet not hold a heavy drawing on the fridge?
independent.a: The force is not strong enough to hold the weight, especially with a gap.

exit.q: Like poles... A) attract B) repel
exit.a: B) repel

exit.q: Big question: how can a magnet push something without touching it?
exit.a: Magnetic force acts at a distance; like poles repel.

lessons.homework: Draw a bar magnet and label N and S. Draw arrows to show two magnets attracting and two repelling.
lessons.send: SEND: coloured N and S cards to match. EAL: attract and repel with hand actions. Stretch: test how far away a magnet can still move a paper clip, in centimetres.

lessons.title: How strong is a magnet? Uses of magnets
lessons.bigQuestion: Is a bigger magnet always a stronger magnet?
objectives: To understand how to compare the strength of magnets and how we use magnets every day
successCriteria: All: count how many paper clips a magnet holds
Most: compare two magnets fairly
Some: explain why the biggest magnet is not always the strongest
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: tally and bar chart of paper clip counts
lessons.smsc: Social: working with an adult and sharing results with the class

keywords.def: how strongly a magnet pulls
look at how things are the same or different
things linked one after another
what we think will happen
pulled by a magnet

hook.text: You have a big magnet and a tiny magnet. Which is stronger? How could you test it fairly?
hook.a: Size does not always tell us. Count how many paper clips each can hold in a chain.

starter.q: Like poles: attract or repel?
Can a magnet work through paper?
Name a magnetic metal.

teach.heading: Test the strength
bullets: Hang a paper clip from the magnet
Add clips one at a time
Count the clips before they fall
teach.note: Model the chain test on camera.

teach.heading: Keep it fair
teach.note: Ask: what must stay the same?

teach.heading: Example results
bullets: More clips means a stronger magnet
teach.note: Point out the small round magnet beat the big flat one.

teach.heading: Magnets we use
teach.note: Ask pupils to find one magnet in their home.

practice.q: Magnet A held 4 clips. Magnet B held 10 clips. Which is stronger?
practice.a: Magnet B: it held more clips.
practice.model: Compare the numbers: 10 is more than 4. More clips held means a stronger pull. So magnet B is stronger.

practice.q: In the bar chart, which magnet was weakest?
practice.a: The fridge magnet (2 clips).

practice.q: Why must the paper clips be the same size?
practice.a: So the test is fair; bigger clips are heavier.

independent.q: Core: Test two magnets at home with the paper clip chain. Record the number of clips for each.
independent.a: Pupils' own results.
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: one clip, then two, then three, until the chain drops. The last number that stayed is the result.

independent.q: Extend: Which magnet was stronger? Was it the bigger one?
independent.a: Pupils' own; the bigger magnet is not always the stronger one.

independent.q: Stretch: Name two uses of magnets in your home and say why a magnet is useful there.
independent.a: For example: fridge door seal keeps the door shut; bag clasp holds the bag closed without a zip.

exit.q: More paper clips held means the magnet is... A) stronger B) weaker
exit.a: A) stronger

exit.q: Big question: is a bigger magnet always a stronger magnet?
exit.a: No. We must test it; some small magnets are very strong.

lessons.homework: Find three uses of magnets at home and draw one of them with a label.
lessons.send: SEND: count clips with an adult; number line to 20. EAL: stronger, weaker, compare. Stretch: draw a bar chart of your results.

lessons.title: Light sources: why do cat's eyes glow?
lessons.bigQuestion: Do cat's eyes really make their own light?
objectives: To understand that we need light to see and that some things give out light while others only reflect it
successCriteria: All: name three light sources
Most: say that dark is the absence of light
Some: explain why cat's eyes and the Moon are not light sources
lessons.crossCurricular: English: Cornerstones companion text question 'Why do cat's eyes glow at night?'
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: Allah made the Sun a lamp and the Moon a reflected light

keywords.def: something that gives out its own light
where there is no light
bounce light off a surface
light enters our eyes
give out light

hook.text: In a room with no light at all, could a cat see a mouse? Could you?
hook.a: No. Cats need some light too. With no light at all, nothing can be seen.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'It is He who made the sun a shining light and the moon a derived light' (Yunus 10:5). The Sun makes its own light; the Moon only shines because it reflects the Sun's light.

starter.q: Name a use of magnets.
starter.a: For example: fridge door, compass, sorting cans.

starter.q: Is the Sun a light source?
What do we need to see?

teach.heading: Light sources
bullets: A light source gives out its own light
The Sun, a torch, a lamp, a candle
teach.note: Ask: which things in your room give out light?

teach.heading: How we see
teach.note: Draw arrows: Sun to book, book to eye. Ask: where does the light start?

teach.heading: Cat's eyes
bullets: A shiny layer reflects light back
teach.note: Cats see well in dim light; a layer at the back of the eye reflects light. Road studs work the same way.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Give 30 seconds.

check.why: A torch gives out its own light. The others reflect light.

practice.q: Is the Moon a light source?
practice.a: No. It reflects light from the Sun.
practice.model: Ask: does it make its own light? The Moon does not. It shines because the Sun's light bounces off it. So it is not a light source.

practice.q: What is dark?
practice.a: When there is no light.

practice.q: Put in order: light enters eye, light leaves Sun, light hits book.
practice.a: Light leaves Sun, light hits book, light enters eye.

independent.q: Core: Go around your home (with an adult). List 4 light sources and 4 things that only reflect light.
independent.a: Light sources: lamp, screen, torch, oven light. Reflect only: mirror, spoon, foil, window.
independent.model: Teacher does two first: a lamp (light source: it gives out light), a spoon (reflects: it only shines when light hits it).

independent.q: Extend: Draw arrows to show how you see a book in a room lit by a lamp.
independent.a: Arrow from lamp to book; arrow from book to eye.

independent.q: Stretch: Why can't you see anything in a sealed dark cupboard?
independent.a: No light can get in, so no light reflects into your eyes.

exit.q: Cat's eyes... A) make light B) reflect light
exit.a: B) reflect light

exit.q: Big question: do cat's eyes really make their own light?
exit.a: No. They reflect light that shines into them.

lessons.homework: Draw your bedroom at night. Label one light source and one thing that reflects light.
lessons.send: SEND: real objects and a torch to sort. EAL: light source, reflect, dark with pictures. Stretch: explain why a mirror looks dark in a dark room.

lessons.title: Reflection: testing reflective materials
lessons.bigQuestion: Which materials are best for keeping walkers safe in the dark?
objectives: To understand that shiny and light-coloured surfaces reflect light well
successCriteria: All: say that a mirror reflects light
Most: test which materials reflect torchlight best
Some: explain why reflective strips are used on bags and coats
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: road safety in the dark
lessons.smsc: Moral: keeping ourselves and others safe

keywords.def: light bouncing off a surface
good at bouncing light back
a very smooth shiny surface that reflects light well
smooth and bright
not shiny

hook.text: Why do road workers, cyclists and school bags have shiny strips on them?
hook.a: The strips reflect car headlights back, so drivers can see them in the dark.

starter.q: Is a mirror a light source?
Name one light source.
starter.a: For example: the Sun, a torch, a lamp.

starter.q: What does 'reflect' mean?

teach.heading: Shiny and dull
bullets: Smooth, shiny surfaces reflect a lot
teach.note: Shine a torch at foil, then at a dark sock on camera.

teach.heading: Our test
bullets: Shine the torch from the same place
teach.note: Fair test: same torch, same distance, same angle.

teach.heading: Safety
bullets: Never shine a torch into eyes
Ask an adult before darkening a room
teach.note: Read the safety card together.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.why: Foil is smooth and shiny, so it reflects the most light.

practice.q: Which reflects more: white paper or black paper?
practice.a: White paper.
practice.model: Think: light or dark colour? White is light. Light colours reflect more light. So white paper reflects more.

practice.q: Why are reflective strips useful on a school bag?
practice.a: They reflect car lights so drivers can see you.

practice.q: Name the fair-test thing we change.
practice.a: The material.

independent.q: Core: In a dim room, shine a torch on 5 materials (foil, white paper, black fabric, a spoon, cardboard). Score each 1 (dull) to 5 (very bright).
independent.a: Pupils' own; foil and spoon score highest, black fabric lowest.
independent.model: Teacher shows the first: torch 30 cm away, shine on foil, it is very bright: score 5.

independent.q: Extend: Which material would you put on a coat for walking at night? Why?
independent.a: A shiny reflective strip or foil-like material: it reflects the most light.

independent.q: Stretch: Why does a mirror show a clear picture but foil does not?
independent.a: The mirror is very smooth, so light bounces back evenly; crumpled foil scatters it.

exit.q: Shiny surfaces reflect... A) more light B) less light
exit.a: A) more light

exit.q: Big question: which materials are best for keeping walkers safe in the dark?
exit.a: Shiny, light or reflective materials such as reflective strips.

lessons.homework: Find two reflective things on coats, bags or shoes at home. Draw them and say how they keep people safe.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-cut material squares and a smiley-face scale. EAL: shiny, dull, reflect. Stretch: test the materials at two distances and compare.

lessons.title: Shadows: how are they made?
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a shadow get bigger when you move closer to the torch?
objectives: To understand that shadows form when an opaque object blocks light
successCriteria: All: say that a shadow forms when light is blocked
Most: sort materials into opaque, translucent and transparent
Some: explain how shadow size changes with distance from the torch
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: measuring shadow height in centimetres
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: shadows remind us of the Sun's movement that Allah controls

keywords.def: a dark shape where light is blocked
lets no light through
lets all light through, so we see clearly
lets some light through
stop something getting past

hook.text: Can a glass of water make a shadow? Can a sheet of paper? Which makes the darker shadow?
hook.a: Clear glass makes a faint shadow; paper makes a darker one. Opaque things block the most light.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Have you not seen how your Lord stretches out the shadow? ... Then We made the sun its guide' (al-Furqan 25:45). Shadows show us that the Sun's light travels in straight lines and is blocked by objects.

starter.q: Is a torch a light source?
Which reflects more: foil or a black sock?
How do we see things?
starter.a: Light bounces off them into our eyes.

teach.heading: Making a shadow
bullets: A dark shadow forms behind it
teach.note: Shine a torch at a cup on camera. Point to the shadow on the wall.

teach.heading: Three kinds of material
teach.note: Use a book, tissue paper and a clear bag.

teach.heading: Closer means bigger
bullets: Object far from torch: small shadow
teach.note: Example results from a toy shadow on a wall.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.why: Wood is opaque: it blocks all the light.

practice.q: A book is opaque. What kind of shadow does it make?
practice.a: A dark shadow: it blocks all the light.
practice.model: Step 1: opaque means no light gets through. Step 2: all the light is blocked. So the shadow is dark.

practice.q: From the table, what happens to the shadow as the toy moves away from the torch?
practice.a: The shadow gets smaller.

practice.q: Is a clear plastic bag opaque, translucent or transparent?
practice.a: Transparent.

independent.q: Core: Make a shadow of a toy on a wall with a torch. Measure the shadow height with the toy 10 cm, 20 cm and 30 cm from the torch.
independent.a: Pupils' own; the shadow gets smaller as the toy moves away from the torch.
independent.model: Teacher shows the first reading: toy 10 cm from torch, mark the top of the shadow on paper, measure with a ruler.

independent.q: Extend: Write a sentence to describe your pattern.
independent.a: The further the toy is from the torch, the smaller the shadow.

independent.q: Stretch: Why is a shadow always the same shape as the object's outline?
independent.a: Light travels in straight lines, so it is blocked in the shape of the object's edges.

exit.q: A material that lets no light through is... A) transparent B) opaque
exit.a: B) opaque

exit.q: Big question: why does a shadow get bigger when you move closer to the torch?
exit.a: The object blocks more of the spreading light when it is closer, so the shadow is bigger.

lessons.homework: Make shadows of three different household objects. Draw them and say whether each object is opaque, translucent or transparent.
lessons.send: SEND: one object and two distances only. EAL: opaque, translucent, transparent on a word mat with pictures. Stretch: predict the shadow height at 40 cm from the pattern.

lessons.title: Shadows in the day and unit quiz

keywords.def: a dark shape where light is blocked
when the Sun appears in the morning
the middle of the day, when the Sun is highest
how long something is
lets no light through

hook.text: In the early morning your shadow is very long. At midday it is short. Why?
hook.a: When the Sun is low, light hits at a slant and shadows are long; when the Sun is high, shadows are short.

islamicLink.text: The times of the daily prayers follow the Sun. The time for 'Asr begins when the length of an object's shadow reaches a set length compared with the object, so Muslims have watched shadows carefully for centuries.

starter.q: Opaque, translucent or transparent: tissue paper?
Which is magnetic: steel or aluminium?
What force slows a toy car on a carpet?

teach.heading: The Sun in the sky
bullets: The Sun seems to move across the sky
It rises in the east, sets in the west
teach.note: Explain: it is the Earth that turns; the Sun seems to move. Never look at the Sun.

teach.heading: Shadow length
teach.note: Example results from a stick in a garden.

teach.heading: Unit quiz: how to answer
teach.note: Quiz in the portal; pupils may use their word mats for spelling.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.why: The Sun is highest at midday, so shadows are shortest.

practice.q: From the chart, when was the shadow longest?
practice.a: At 9 am (180 cm).
practice.model: Find the tallest bar: 9 am, 180 cm. That is the longest shadow, when the Sun was low.

practice.q: Why are shadows long in the morning?
practice.a: The Sun is low in the sky.

practice.q: Is the Sun really moving across the sky?
practice.a: No, the Earth turns; the Sun only seems to move.

independent.q: Core (unit quiz, in the portal): 8 questions on friction, magnets, light sources, reflection and shadows.
independent.a: Answers in the teacher key: e.g. friction slows; steel magnetic; Moon reflects; opaque blocks light; like poles repel.
independent.model: Teacher goes through question 1 first: 'Which surface has more friction, ice or carpet?' Carpet, because it is rougher.

independent.q: Extend: Explain one thing you learned about magnets that surprised you.
independent.a: For example: aluminium is a metal but it is not magnetic.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why a sundial can tell the time.
independent.a: The Sun's position changes during the day, so the shadow moves round and points to the time.

exit.q: Shadows are shortest... A) at midday B) in the evening
exit.a: A) at midday

exit.q: Big question: why does your shadow change during the day?
exit.a: The Sun's position in the sky changes, so the angle of the light changes.

lessons.homework: With an adult, mark the shadow of a bottle on paper by a sunny window at two times of day. Is it longer or shorter later?
lessons.send: SEND: quiz read aloud; picture options. EAL: morning, midday, evening with a Sun picture. Stretch: predict the shadow length at 5 pm and explain.
